extracted.intended_audience: students learning news writing / journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises for newsroom-style editing: paragraphing, sentence-level grammar, and stylistic corrections used in a news-writing textbook. Students are asked to rewrite bad examples, indicate paragraph breaks, and correct pronoun, verb, coordination, and ellipsis faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate paragraph breaks in stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate the places at which paragraphs should be made in the following stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must read continuous copy (examples include human-interest and news narratives such as 'CHARACTER INDICATED BY THE LIPS', 'FASHION MODEL MARRIES ALL IN BLACK', and several accident/crime vignettes) and decide logical paragraph boundaries — e.g., separate lead/summary facts from background, separate actions or changes in time/location, and break long descriptive passages into manageable units. Examples on the page show long run-on descriptive passages where paragraphing would improve readability and clarity; rewrite with paragraph breaks that group related facts, quotes, and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate stories: rewrite bad ones and justify good ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The following stories are good and bad. Rewrite any that need correction. Show why the others are good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must judge whole stories for correctness and news-writing quality: identify factual ambiguities, grammatical errors, awkward or hyperbolic phrasing, and structural problems; perform rewrites to correct these faults; and explain (briefly) why other items are acceptable as published. The page provides many short items (accidents, crimes, social notices) to practice distinguishing publishable copy from copy needing revision. Pay attention to accuracy of names, chronology, clarity of who-did-what-to-whom, and avoidance of sensationalistic or inflated language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns — identify and correct incorrect pronoun usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A. The following sentences contain pronouns incorrectly used. Indicate and correct the faults in each sentence. (Paragraphs 147-149.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct pronoun-antecedent agreement (singular/plural), case (subject/object), ambiguous antecedents, and inappropriate generic 'they' vs 'he/she' uses. Examples on the page include: mismatches like 'each member ... is expected to have their respective duties' (should be 'his or her'), improper collective references, and unclear references where 'they' could refer to multiple possible antecedents. Students rewrite sentences to make antecedents clear and pronouns grammatically consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbs — correct tense and subject-verb agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: B. Correct the verbs in the following sentences (paragraphs 160-163).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix errors of subject-verb agreement (singular/plural), improper tense usage, incorrect auxiliary verbs, misplaced passive or participial constructions, and errors caused by intervening phrases. Examples include plural subjects with singular verbs or vice versa ('An eighteen-year-old girl ... were arraigned' should be 'was arraigned'), awkward tense constructions ('had expected to have got' -> 'had expected to get' or 'expected to have gotten'), and wrong verb forms after participial phrases. Ensure verbs agree with their grammatical subjects and that tense conveys the correct sequence of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and subordination — fix sentence-structure faults
rubrics_metrics.description: C. The following sentences illustrate faults in coordination and subordination. Correct the errors. (Mainly paragraphs 154-155.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and correct run-on sentences, comma splices, faulty parallelism, misplaced or dangling clauses, and unclear clause attachment. Examples include sentences that string unrelated clauses together, sentences that fail to subordinate dependent material properly, and lists that break parallel structure. Revisions should produce clear principal clauses with properly attached modifiers and parallel elements (e.g., convert awkward multi-clause run-ons into two or more sentences or use proper subordinating conjunctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis faults — identify and correct errors due to omitted elements
rubrics_metrics.description: D. The following sentences contain errors due principally to faulty ellipsis. Point out the faults in ellipsis and correct all errors. (Mainly paragraph 166.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct sentences where words omitted (ellipsis) produce ambiguity or ungrammatical constructions: missing verbs, omitted subjects, incorrect comparative or correlative structures, or incorrectly assumed words. Examples on the page: omitted auxiliary verbs, missing relative pronouns or prepositions, and truncated clauses that make meaning unclear. Reconstruct sentences to supply the missing elements so meaning and grammar are restored.
